chunks: Ahmad ibn Mihran, from Muhammad ibn Ali, from Musa ibn Sa'dan, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, from Abu Ibrahim (peace be upon him), regarding the words of God, Mighty and Majestic:
'He revives the earth after its death'

He said: He does not revive it with the drops of rain, but rather God sends men who revive justice, and thus the earth is revived through the revival of justice. And the establishment of God's prescribed punishments is more beneficial for the earth than the drops of rain for forty days.

key_terms.إِحْيَاءُ الْأَرْضِ: Revival of the earth — interpreted spiritually/socially as revival through just governance rather than literal agricultural revival
key_terms.الْحَدُّ: al-Hadd — prescribed limit/punishment in Islamic law (hudud); the plural hudud refers to fixed penalties for specific offenses
key_terms.الْعَدْلُ: al-'Adl — justice; the Imam's revival of justice is the true meaning of the earth's revival
key_terms.الْقَطْرُ: al-Qatr — drops of rain; used here as a symbol of natural, material revival

ai.seo_question: What does it mean that God revives the earth after its death in Quran 57:17, according to Imam al-Kazim?
ai.summary: Imam Musa al-Kazim (AS), the 7th Imam, provides an esoteric commentary on Quran 57:17, reinterpreting the 'revival of the earth after its death' as a metaphor for the establishment of justice through divinely-sent leaders. He argues that the application of God's prescribed punishments (hudud) has greater benefit for society than even forty days of rain. This teaching reflects the Shia understanding that the true reviver of humanity is the just Imam who establishes divine law.
